Corn_Common Rust.name: Common Rust
symptoms: Small, round to elongated reddish-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf
Pustules burst and release powdery rust-colored spores
Severe infection makes leaves yellow and dry early
Corn_Common Rust.causes: Fungus (Puccinia sorghi). Spores travel by wind and it spreads fastest in cool, humid weather with heavy dew.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide if infection starts early and is spreading
Ask your local agriculture office for the right product and dose for your area
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids
Sow early and scout fields regularly in cool, humid weather

Corn_Gray Leaf Spot.name: Gray Leaf Spot
symptoms: Narrow, rectangular tan to gray spots running parallel to the leaf veins
Spots join together and large parts of the leaf dry out
Corn_Gray Leaf Spot.causes: Fungus (Cercospora zeae-maydis) that survives in old corn residue. Warm, humid weather and dense crops make it worse.
treatment: Apply a recommended foliar fungicide early if the disease is spreading on upper leaves
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Rotate with non-host crops
Bury or remove old corn residue
Use resistant hybrids and avoid very dense planting

Corn_Healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease signs on this leaf
treatment: No treatment needed
prevention: Keep checking the field regularly
Use balanced fertilizer and proper irrigation

Corn_Northern Leaf Blight.name: Northern Leaf Blight
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions on the leaves
Lesions grow and join, and leaves dry out from the lower part of the plant upward
Corn_Northern Leaf Blight.causes: Fungus (Exserohilum turcicum). It survives in crop residue and spreads in moderate temperatures with long periods of leaf wetness.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide if the disease reaches upper leaves before or around flowering
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids
Rotate crops and manage corn residue

Cotton_Alternaria Leaf Spot.name: Alternaria Leaf Spot
symptoms: Small brown to gray circular spots, often with ring-like patterns
Spots can dry and fall out, and leaves may drop early
Cotton_Alternaria Leaf Spot.causes: Fungus (Alternaria species). It is worse in warm, humid weather and in plants stressed by poor nutrition, especially low potassium.
treatment: Use a recommended fungicide if the spots are spreading
Correct nutrient problems, especially potassium
prevention: Keep plants well fed and avoid water stress
Rotate crops and remove old crop residue

Cotton_Bacterial Blight.name: Bacterial Blight
symptoms: Angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that are limited by the veins and turn brown or black
Dark lesions can appear on stems and bolls, and bolls may rot
Cotton_Bacterial Blight.causes: Bacterium (Xanthomonas citri pv. malvacearum). It spreads through infected seed, crop residue, and rain splash.
treatment: There is no complete cure once the plant is infected
Copper-based sprays may slow the spread, so check the recommendation with your local agriculture office
Remove and destroy badly infected plants and residue
prevention: Use certified disease-free (acid-delinted) seed
Plant resistant varieties and rotate crops

Cotton_Fusarium Wilt.name: Fusarium Wilt
symptoms: Yellowing and wilting of leaves, often starting on one side of the plant
Stunted growth
Brown color inside the stem when it is cut open
Cotton_Fusarium Wilt.causes: Soil-borne fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum). It is worse in sandy soils and where root-knot nematodes are present.
treatment: There is no effective cure for infected plants
Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce spread
prevention: Plant wilt-resistant varieties
Control nematodes and rotate with non-host crops
Keep soil nutrition balanced, especially potassium

Cotton_Healthy Leaf.name: Healthy Leaf
symptoms: No visible disease signs on this leaf
treatment: No treatment needed
prevention: Keep checking the field regularly
Use balanced fertilizer and proper irrigation

Cotton_Verticillium Wilt.name: Verticillium Wilt
symptoms: Yellow patches between the leaf veins, with leaf edges turning brown
Wilting and early leaf drop
Dark streaks inside the stem
Cotton_Verticillium Wilt.causes: Soil-borne fungus (Verticillium dahliae) that can stay in the soil for years. It is more active in cooler weather.
treatment: There is no effective cure for infected plants
Remove and destroy infected plants and residue
prevention: Plant tolerant varieties
Rotate with cereals or other non-host crops
Avoid too much nitrogen and over-irrigation

Wheat_Black Rust.name: Black Rust (Stem Rust)
symptoms: Dark reddish-brown to black, rough pustules on stems, leaf sheaths and leaves
Weak stems and shriveled grain in severe cases
Wheat_Black Rust.causes: Fungus (Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici). Spores spread long distances by wind and it develops in warm, humid conditions.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide quickly at the first signs
Report severe outbreaks to your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Sow on time and scout fields regularly

Wheat_Blast.name: Wheat Blast
symptoms: Part of the head turns white (bleached) above a dark lesion on the stalk of the head
Grains are shriveled or not formed
Wheat_Blast.causes: Fungus (Magnaporthe oryzae, Triticum pathotype). It can be carried on seed and is favored by warm, wet weather during heading.
treatment: Fungicide protection works best when applied at heading, as recommended locally
Report suspected wheat blast to your local agriculture office, because it is a serious disease
prevention: Use clean, certified (and treated) seed
Plant resistant varieties
Avoid sowing dates that make heading coincide with warm, wet weather

Wheat_Brown Rust.name: Brown Rust (Leaf Rust)
symptoms: Small, round orange-brown pustules scattered on the upper leaf surface
Leaves dry out early in severe cases
Wheat_Brown Rust.causes: Fungus (Puccinia triticina). Spores spread by wind and it develops in mild temperatures with moisture on the leaves.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide early if the disease is spreading
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Sow on time and remove volunteer wheat plants

Wheat_Common Root Rot.name: Common Root Rot
symptoms: Brown to dark-brown color on the crown, roots and lower stem
Stunted plants, early ripening and white, empty heads
Wheat_Common Root Rot.causes: Fungus (Bipolaris sorokiniana) that lives in soil, residue and seed. Drought and other stress make it worse.
treatment: There is no effective cure in a standing crop
Improve irrigation and drainage to reduce plant stress
prevention: Use treated, clean seed
Rotate crops and avoid drought stress
Keep soil fertility balanced

Wheat_Fusarium Head Blight.name: Fusarium Head Blight (Scab)
symptoms: Parts of the head turn white early while the rest stays green
Pink-orange fungal growth on the head in wet weather
Shriveled, pale, chalky grain
Wheat_Fusarium Head Blight.causes: Fungus (Fusarium graminearum). Rain or humid weather during flowering spreads it, and old corn residue makes it worse.
treatment: Fungicide works only if applied at flowering, so timing is important. Check the recommendation with your local agriculture office
Clean out shriveled grain at harvest
Do not use heavily infected grain for food or animal feed, because it can contain toxins
prevention: Avoid planting wheat right after corn
Use less susceptible varieties and manage crop residue

Wheat_Healthy.name: Healthy
symptoms: No visible disease signs on this leaf
treatment: No treatment needed
prevention: Keep checking the field regularly
Use balanced fertilizer and proper irrigation

Wheat_Leaf Blight.name: Leaf Blight
symptoms: Brown to tan blotches on the leaves that grow and join together
Leaves dry out early
Wheat_Leaf Blight.causes: Several fungi can cause leaf blight in wheat. It spreads through seed and crop residue and is worse in warm, humid weather.
treatment: Use a recommended foliar fungicide if the disease is moving up to the top leaves
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Use certified, treated seed
Rotate crops, manage residue and avoid late sowing
Keep fertilizer balanced

Wheat_Mildew.name: Powdery Mildew
symptoms: White to gray powdery growth on the upper leaf surface
Older patches turn yellow-brown with tiny black dots
Wheat_Mildew.causes: Fungus (Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici). It is favored by cool, humid, cloudy weather, thick crops and too much nitrogen.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide if the disease is spreading to upper leaves
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Avoid too much nitrogen and very dense sowing

Wheat_Septoria.name: Septoria Leaf Blotch
symptoms: Yellow to brown blotches, usually starting on the lower leaves
Tiny black dots inside the blotches
Wheat_Septoria.causes: Fungus (Zymoseptoria tritici) that survives on crop residue and spreads by rain splash in cool, wet weather.
treatment: Fungicide is most useful to protect the upper leaves, if recommended locally
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Rotate crops and manage residue
Avoid very early sowing

Wheat_Smut.name: Smut
symptoms: Heads filled with black powdery spore masses instead of grain
Infected heads often come out earlier than healthy ones
Wheat_Smut.causes: Smut fungi. In loose smut the fungus is carried inside the seed, so it passes from one season to the next.
treatment: There is no cure for infected plants
Carefully remove infected heads in a bag before the spores spread, and destroy them
prevention: Use certified seed and a recommended seed treatment
Plant resistant varieties

Wheat_Tan spot.name: Tan Spot
symptoms: Tan to brown oval spots, often with a yellow border and a dark spot in the center
Spots join together and the leaf dries out
Wheat_Tan spot.causes: Fungus (Pyrenophora tritici-repentis) that survives in wheat residue. It is worse when wheat follows wheat.
treatment: Use a recommended foliar fungicide if the disease is moving up to the top leaves
Confirm product and dose with your local agriculture office
prevention: Rotate crops and avoid wheat after wheat
Manage crop residue and use certified seed

Wheat_Yellow Rust.name: Yellow Rust (Stripe Rust)
symptoms: Yellow-orange powdery pustules in stripes along the leaf veins
Leaves dry out and yield drops in severe cases
Wheat_Yellow Rust.causes: Fungus (Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici). Spores spread quickly by wind and it develops in cool, humid weather.
treatment: Apply a recommended fungicide quickly at the first signs, because it spreads fast
Report outbreaks to your local agriculture office
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Avoid late sowing and too much nitrogen
Scout fields regularly from early growth stages
